Monthly visits declined steadily through H1 SimilarWeb: 354K in January, 334K in February, 308K in March, 295K in April, a partial recovery to 328K in May, then a violent reversal to 597K in June. That June spike was driven almost entirely by one account. Session behavior confirms the cashier read: bounce between 49% and 57%, 2.0 to 2.5 pages per visit, average duration around two minutes. Nobody is reading their blog. They are depositing.

The one thing to remember

PayRetailers' H1 2026 growth story is one CS2 skins-gambling account. Underneath it, their regulated broker book is eroding month over month.

The client roster, read from the wire.

Every domain below routed checkout traffic to payretailers.com in H1 2026. Merchant status is high confidence; corporate ownership is medium confidence where entities are offshore.

The book splits roughly 60% binary options / CFD / forex brokers, 20% sportsbook and casino (the 1xBet family, Stake, Sol Casino), plus lottery, skins gambling, and one adult creator platform. A large cluster shares the billing.trade.[brand].com URL pattern: offshore brokers on a common white-label stack, structured through Nevis, Cyprus, and St. Kitts shells, several explicitly Brazil-targeted with Portuguese frontends. Only one client is publicly confirmed by PayRetailers itself: a 1xBet LATAM expansion case study on their own site. Everything else is traffic-inferred.

Three things the monthly series adds that the aggregate hid. First, the 1xBet Mexico correction: the -89% on 1xbet.com.mx in the aggregate export is a domain migration, with volume moving to the 1-x.mx mirror and the 1xlite satellites in the same weeks, the signature of Mexican regulator domain-blocking rather than a lost account. It comes off the displacement list. Second, the decline of the regulated-broker book is monotonic, not noisy: IQ Option steps down almost every month and Quotex is functionally gone by June at 1.4%. Third, skin.club's 26% is one month old: April's 11.3% collapsed to 3.5% in May before the June spike, so their new flagship account is also their most volatile. A note on method: each monthly export caps at roughly the top 50 referrers, so long-tail accounts from the aggregate (Stake, casatrade, Deriv) sit below the monthly cutoff; their trends remain aggregate-only.

Confirmed anchor

1xBet is the only merchant PayRetailers names publicly, via their own LATAM expansion case study. It anchors the entire traffic-inference method.

Argentina's +825% traffic growth is the second story of the half. No PayRetailers announcement explains it. The most plausible driver is Argentina's province-by-province iGaming liberalization: ALEA (the Argentine State Lotteries Association) reports 49% of Argentine players now use digital wallets versus 23% who prefer in-person betting. That is market tailwind, and it is available to us too. Peru meanwhile fell 40%, and their status page logged Peru payout maintenance twice in the period (Jun 27 and Jul 1).

Risk flag on their book

Revenue mix is rotating away from regulated brokers toward skins gambling and anonymous white-label binaries. That is a compliance profile a BCB-licensed competitor can attack on trust alone.

Rails, methods, and the Praxis cascade.

Outbound traffic from the checkout reveals the payin mix. Inbound from ccport.praxispay.com reveals something more interesting.

ccport.praxispay.com is a top-6 inbound referrer, and terminal.praxispay.com plus api-terminal.praxispay.com appear on the outbound side SimilarWeb. PayRetailers is integrated as a payment rail inside Praxis Tech's cascading cashier. They receive volume two ways: directly from their own merchants, and downstream as one option inside an orchestration layer we already profiled in the Praxis brief (v14). When Praxis routes around them, that volume disappears without any merchant churning.

Method mix read

Colombia bank transfer (PSE, Nequi) plus Chile (Webpay, Khipu) dominate visible payins; Brazil runs native Pix through Transfeera. Cards are marginal in the redirect data.

The decomposition changes the read. Total measured search clicks in June: ~140 across all 520 variants, and every single one landed on the Colombia funnel via the two Colombian acquirer brands. The other ~500 variants form a global PSP conquest blanket: Adyen, Airwallex, 2Checkout, Afterpay, Affirm, and Brazil's AbacatePay, all bid at near-zero delivery. Someone set up a keyword dragnet across the entire payments landscape and let it idle. Meanwhile the ePayco CPC jumped from $0.24 in the H1 aggregate to $3.39 in June: either ePayco started defending its brand, or a third bidder entered that auction. Colombia is the only paid front where money actually moves.

The display campaign: World Cup banners on the Payout Wound

SimilarWeb's Recent Ads panel caught a display flight in mid-May 2026 that neither the Semrush export nor the Google Ads Transparency Center surfaced: banner creative in 640×360, 970×250, and 300×250, each seen for single-day flights on May 13 and 14, pushing a downloadable World Cup payments guide. Two messages carry the campaign: "70% of World Cup payments will be mobile. Is your checkout ready?" and, more interesting for us, "88% of users switch providers after a bad payment experience. During the World Cup, every second counts." They are spending money to teach the market that payment friction drives provider switching. That is our Payout Wound thesis, in their creative, with their budget.

What the live channels added

Google Ads Transparency Center confirms the verified advertiser as PAYRETAILERS GROUP, S.L.U., with 21 creatives all-time and 6 active in the last 30 days, all search text ads in PT, ES, and EN with generic gateway copy. The Center does not expose keywords, so the Stone, PayU, and ePayco conquest bids can be neither confirmed nor refuted there; the Semrush export stands as the only keyword-level source, and the active PT and ES spend is consistent with it. Meta Ad Library returns zero results for PayRetailers in any country. Their entire paid acquisition stack is Google search plus short display bursts plus events. No Meta, no LinkedIn ads observed.

Branded demand outweighs unbranded, meaning merchants already know who they are and search by name. Social referral traffic is YouTube plus WhatsApp Web (18.8%) plus Telegram Web (14.1%): onboarding and affiliate flows over messaging, not consumer social. SEO overlap competitors in the period: PagoNxt (Santander), CDI Global, Payteria. Similarweb affinity puts Nuvei at 1.00, their closest structural twin. The live pass also located their Instagram: @pay.retailers, 5,458 followers, 141 posts, an employer-branding and sponsorship-trophy channel (CONMEBOL Sudamericana, SLAR highlights) with negligible merchant-facing reach, mirroring the LinkedIn Bre-B and World Cup arcs.

Read the intent

Search conquest chases generic e-commerce acquiring while the display burst courts entertainment audiences with switching math. The ad account is arguing with itself about who the customer is.

Gift for our messaging

Their own creative validates the Payout Wound: 88% of users switch providers after a bad payment experience. We can cite the market education they paid for.

Reputation, both sides of the glass

Consumer side, Trustpilot: 2.1 of 5, 71% one-star, top mention chip "Fraud." Every 2026-dated review is a consumer scam victim whose deposit to an offshore broker rode PayRetailers rails: an April pair from Chile describing roughly US$5,000 lost to a scheme called ALGOBI via a PayRetailers Chile account at Banco Itaú, and a January review from Colombia alleging payment links generated through Pago Digital Colombia S.A.S. for a scam broker. Older merchant-side reviews describe settlement freezes in payout-friction language, supporting the Payout Wound thesis.

Employee side, Glassdoor, now fully read: 3.1 of 5 across 72 reviews, 55% would recommend, CEO approval 52%, company outlook positive for only 47%. The category scores tell the real story: compensation 3.6 and diversity 3.5 at the top, culture and career progression at 3.1, and executive leadership at 2.8, the lowest-rated dimension. The June and July 2026 reviews cluster around one theme from 3-plus-year veterans: one ex-project manager titles it "empresa caótica en el último año", a data analyst cites poor communication, a manager cites good pay but unclear growth. That is the workforce describing the same integration digestion the hiring data shows. Glassdoor's own FAQ module now auto-surfaces a question about 2026 layoffs ("despidos"), meaning enough reviews mention them to generate the entry. Interview data: 28 records, easy difficulty, and a notably split 50% positive versus 46% negative candidate experience.

The reputational math

A book that is 60% offshore binaries produces scam-victim complaints naming your bank accounts in public reviews. Their client mix is now their compliance surface. Ours is the counter-pitch.

The strategic read for LaFinteca.

Where they win, where they bleed, and the sequence of moves.

Reveal one: the China corridor is an iGaming corridor

The CCO's China post (permalink, 58 reactions) reads like relationship theater until you check who went with him. His travel companion, Jorge Ignacio Fiorentino, is Sr. Sales Manager LATAM with iGaming Business Development in his title, visible in the comment thread where he celebrates growing PayRetailers' presence in China. A week of meetings with Chinese holdings "operating in and expanding into Latin America," fronted by an iGaming BD lead, means one thing: they are hunting the Chinese-owned operator ecosystem behind LATAM betting and gaming brands. Torres Velat has done business in China since 2014 (Ant Financial is on his CV), his headline now includes APAC, and the post closes with a standing public offer to any Chinese platform needing LATAM rails.

Why this matters to us: a meaningful share of LATAM-facing gaming brands trace to Chinese capital, and several sit in or near our Mexico shortlist. If PayRetailers formalizes a China desk, they intercept those operators upstream, before the brands ever surface in LATAM sales pipelines. The counter is unglamorous and concrete: map beneficial ownership across our MX and BR operator pipeline for Chinese-held groups, flag which of our existing intel targets have Asian holding structures, and decide whether LaFinteca needs a Mandarin-capable BD motion or a partner who has one. The corridor is real, it is early, and today exactly one competitor is publicly building it.

FIG 10 · The tell is in the comments: Fiorentino, Sr. Sales Manager LATAM · iGaming BD, was the traveling party.

Reveal two: the conversion narrative is a funded campaign, not a post

Sequence the evidence and a coordinated campaign appears. April 21: blog post, five strategies to boost LATAM payment conversion. May 27: blog post on local acquiring, publishing a branded graphic that claims 20–45% approval for cross-border versus 60–80% for local acquiring. Mid-May: the World Cup display burst teaching that 88% of users switch providers after a bad payment experience. Early July: the CCO post (permalink) with the sharpest version: 98% of checkout arrivals attempt to pay, "The problem is not the user," and the failure mechanics named: desktop timeouts on mobile traffic, callbacks that never resolve, payload errors repeating across every bank in a country. Claimed outcome: 60% versus 87% conversion, same method, same country, same merchant type.

The comment thread shows the campaign converting: a Global VP of Digital Payments asks to reconnect and hear their approach, and a fintech entrepreneur openly asks for commercial help. Inbound, in public, from a LinkedIn post. Three exposures in their argument are ours to attack: their numbers are unsourced marketing claims (no methodology, no sample definition, no per-country split), their proof is self-referential, and their reputation surface (Trustpilot 2.1, scam-victim reviews naming their own bank accounts) contradicts a trust-and-reliability pitch. The move: publish a LaFinteca approval-rate benchmark with named methodology and per-rail transparency, arm Rafa's team with a conversion-diagnostic first call that quantifies the merchant's own failure modes, and time it before this narrative hardens into category truth. Their content machine taught the market to care about approval rates. We should be the ones who answer the question rigorously.

Where they win: skins gambling, the white-label binary factory, Chile operations, and orchestration reach through both the Praxis cascade and the Celeris acquisition. Where they bleed: every marquee regulated broker is shrinking monotonically (IQ Option 27% to 8.6% across six months, XTB fading, Quotex at 1.4% and functionally churned), Deriv is gone entirely, and Brazil is 57% of everything, concentrated on Transfeera Pix and offshore binaries at exactly the moment Brazilian regulators are tightening around that segment.

01
Attack the churn list · 0–30 days
Deriv (win-back, already off PayRetailers), Quotex (1.4% in June, effectively out the door), IQ Option, XTB. Lead with approval rates and settlement terms. Escalate any account showing continued decline in the next monthly pull.
02

stake.mx-style regulated casino accounts in Mexico are a clean fit. skin.club requires a risk-appetite decision before any approach; validate first.

Position the BCB license as the trust wedge in Brazil. Stand up Argentina province-level coverage to ride the same digital-wallet shift driving their +825%.
04
Counter-program the ads
They bid on acquirer brands. We bid on "payretailers" plus broker and iGaming payment terms, the verticals where they are strongest yet visibly eroding.
Pitch angle · churned brokers
Your LATAM payin share on PayRetailers rails fell every month this half. We are the BCB-licensed operator built only for digital entertainment, and we will prove the approval-rate delta on your own traffic in 30 days.
Monitoring cadence
Re-pull Similarweb referrers monthly. Reassess when any single account exceeds 25% of referral share, or when a top-10 broker drops more than 30% in a month: that is the displacement window opening.

One account up, a whole vertical down.

PayRetailers' H1 2026 looks healthy only because skin.club is carrying it. Underneath, the regulated broker book that made their name is shrinking every month, Deriv already walked, and their ad money is chasing generic e-commerce instead of defending the niche. That is a competitor exposing its core verticals while distracted, with hiring near-frozen, a 2.1 Trustpilot, and a press room silent since October. LaFinteca's move is surgical: take the churning brokers now, contest Mexico casino accounts next, enter Argentina while their bench is thin, and claim the conversion argument before their CCO finishes building it.
